question: According to Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and related EU legislation on hygiene, blood resulting from the slaughter of farm animals is subject to the rules governing animal byproducts. This also applies to the one-time slaughter of an animal on the farm of origin under EU rules, where the blood must be handled in a controlled manner.

In contrast, when hunting wild game, the blood can typically remain in the wild, even though the meat is also intended for human consumption. Strict hygiene protocols are entirely understandable in large slaughterhouses or intensive livestock operations. However, for family farms that slaughter one or two animals a year out in the open, the question arises as to whether these requirements are proportionate.
Can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
On the basis of what scientific or hygiene findings is blood from the one-time slaughter of a farm animal subject to stricter rules than blood from hunted wild game intended for human consumption?
Did the Commission assess the proportionality of these requirements in relation to small family farms that only occasionally slaughter livestock when drafting the legislation?

As part of a future revision of rules on hygiene or animal by-products, is the Commission considering the creation of a more proportionate regime for small farms without compromising food safety, animal health or environmental protection?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) Wild game hunting is inherently unpredictable, and blood dispersal in such cases is typically minimal. In contrast, the on-farm slaughter of farmed animals can be planned under controlled hygienic conditions, enabling systematic risk mitigation such as preventing pathogen transmission to humans or other animals through blood.

EU food hygiene rules do not apply to the on-farm slaughter of farmed animals for private domestic consumption. When blood is intended for human consumption, it must be handled under strict hygiene conditions according to Regulation (EC) No 853/20041. If these requirements cannot be met, the blood must be excluded from the food chain.

Only then Regulation (EC) No 1069/20092 on animal by-products not intended for human consumption starts to apply regarding the collection and disposal of blood. The principle of proportionality was integral to the development of the EU rules, which recognise that even occasional on-farm slaughter must adhere to core hygiene standards to prevent disease spread and safeguard human health.

The Commission regularly reviews EU legislation on food hygiene and on animal by-products to improve practicality without compromising safety. Additionally, Member States may adapt certain EU food hygiene requirements to preserve traditional methods of food production or accommodate businesses in regions with specific geographic constraints.
Such adaptations must be notified to the Commission in advance and must not pose a risk to public health.
1 Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 laying down

specific hygiene rules for food of animal origin (OJ L 139, 30.4.2004, pp. 55–205). 2 Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 October 2009 laying down health rules as regards animal by-products and derived products not intended for human consumption and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002 (Animal by-products Regulation) (OJ L 300, 14.11.2009, pp. 1–33).
